lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: know the excretory products of the lungs, kidneys and skin (organs of excretion)

primer.text: Respiration and protein breakdown quietly generate chemicals your body cannot store. You have already seen urea appear as the liver's product; here you meet excretion proper — the definition, the reasons a build-up would damage cells, and the three organs that divide the removal work between them.

modules.title: Why the Body Must Excrete
sourceHeadings: The Need for Excretion in Humans
modules.opening: Every working cell leaves behind refuse: carbon dioxide and water from respiration, urea from surplus amino acids. Excretion is the removal of these metabolic wastes together with anything toxic or simply present in excess. Carbon dioxide dissolves in cell water to form an acid that slows the enzymes running metabolism; waste-laden fluids drag water out of cells by osmosis; and internal storage space is finite and needed for useful molecules, not rubbish.
keyPoints: Excretion removes metabolic waste, toxic materials and substances present in excess.
Aerobic respiration in cells yields carbon dioxide and water.
The liver converts surplus amino acids into urea.
Dissolved carbon dioxide acidifies cell water and slows enzyme activity.
Concentrated body fluids pull water out of cells by osmosis and derail their chemistry.

low.restatement: Cells make waste; excretion is the removal of that waste before it harms the body.
low.analogy: Empty a bin regularly and the room stays usable; let it overflow and everything nearby suffers.
low.examPointer: Name all three damage routes — acidity, osmotic drag and storage crowding — when asked why waste is dangerous.

medium.restatement: Excretion clears the products of metabolism; egestion clears undigested food.
medium.analogy: One is taking out the rubbish you made inside the house; the other is sending back the food you never cooked.
medium.examPointer: Do not offer faeces as an excretory product; examiners penalise that classic slip.

modules.title: The Organs of Excretion
modules.opening: Three organs divide the excretory work between them. The kidneys take urea, surplus ions and water and send them out as urine; the lungs exhale carbon dioxide with some water vapour; the skin sweats out salts, water and a trace of urea. Blood arriving at the kidneys carries the urea the liver has made; the lungs push used air out with every breath; and the skin's sweat evaporates from the surface, lifting its cargo away.
keyPoints: The kidneys excrete urea, excess ions and water in urine.
The lungs excrete carbon dioxide and water vapour during exhalation.
The skin excretes excess mineral ions, water and a little urea in sweat.
Urea reaches the kidney by blood from the liver, its site of manufacture.
Matching each waste to its organ is a standard examination demand.

low.restatement: Kidneys, lungs and skin each carry a defined share of the excretory load.
low.analogy: Think of three exits from a building, each signed for a different kind of traffic.
low.examPointer: Practise pairing organ to product without mixing the lists up.

medium.restatement: Lungs take carbon dioxide and some water; kidneys take urea, ions and water; skin takes salts and water.
medium.analogy: Three bins at the kerb: one for gas, one for liquid waste, one for salty overflow.
medium.examPointer: Learn the pairings as a table; questions often ask for organ and product together.

glossary.definition: The removal of metabolic waste, toxic materials and substances in excess of requirements from the body.
The nitrogen-rich waste the liver makes from surplus amino acids; excreted by the kidneys in urine.
The passing out of undigested food, which never entered cells and is therefore not excretion.
